doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Deciding on music: supportive parents and Manhattan School of Music plans
summary: Schoenberg says music felt pre-ordained, describes his New Jersey high school band director and acceptance at Manhattan School of Music in 1976, and his parents' support.

bands.name: Manhattan School of Music jazz band

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive. I’m very pleased to have Loren Schoenberg here today. And I read through your resume, it only took a half an hour.

Bu-dump-bump is right. But all the things you’ve done, I don’t like to bring myself into this but I can personally relate to cause I’ve done a few of them and I know they have required different talents. You started out playing the piano, right? Did you have a point in your teens where you said to yourself dammit, I’m going to be a musician. I’m going to make a living as a musician?

Well I don’t know how to say it. It was almost like pre-ordained or natural for me that this happened. I’m the youngest of three children and sometimes I think the youngest child they say is spoiled or has more options because maybe the parents had other experiences with the older children or something like that. So I evinced a talent for music early on, not a great talent but just I loved to play and I was always playing. And my high school band director had been a music theory major at Manhattan School of Music. And I really kind of cottoned to music theory, for whatever reason, and maybe because he was a great teacher in high school, and we had music theory. This was a normal high school, this was not an arts school, it was just Fairlawn High School in Bergen County, New Jersey, and somehow the career that my band director had had of becoming a music theory major, he had gone to Manhattan School of Music, somehow I kind of fell into that, that that was going to become my goal. And then there were no jazz degrees in those days, not really jazz programs so to speak. Juilliard had no jazz whatsoever, and Manhattan School of Music did have a good jazz band led by Rusty Dedrick, and a good faculty, and so I wound up being accepted to Manhattan School of Music. I guess we’re jumping ahead a little bit here. But I wound up being accepted there in 1976 as a theory major and piano minor. But the funny thing was that my parents, you know my parents were very supportive. I never even contemplated doing anything else. And they let me do that. It wasn’t as though well, like a lot of, I mean there was a kid lived down the street from me, Harry Ballan, much more talented than I am, played Brahms and played the
wonderful piano, and he was a year younger than me, than I. And so but his parents made him get a law degree. And I think that was probably how it was for most kids, but it wasn’t like that for me.
Yeah. They want you to have the, even if you go into music some of them want you to have the fall-back-on.
Right? Get that teaching degree or whatever.
Right. So that was a real leap of faith on my parents I guess. I was very lucky with my parents, which I can tell you more about.
